blocks.text: The exchange between the accusers and Pilate is not simply a private religious dispute. John places the authority to impose the death penalty within Roman prefectural power, while portraying negotiation between local leaders and the governor. An inscription independently preserves Pilate’s name and title as prefect of Judea, though it does not verify the particular hearing dialogue or identify the praetorium’s location.

In this scene, the expression often rendered “the Jews” should not automatically be read as referring to all Jewish people. Its referent can vary with context, including particular authorities, Judeans, festival crowds, or Jewish people more broadly. That care matters here because Pilate’s repeated use of “King of the Jews” places Jesus’ kingship within a politically charged exchange shaped by imperial power.

Across the passion narrative, John depicts conflict involving particular Jewish leaders and participants, while Pilate orders a Roman crucifixion carried out by Roman soldiers. The narrative therefore cannot support claims of collective Jewish guilt or deicide.
